questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Openings that name a disagreement
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an opening that names what is in dispute from one that names who holds it
questions.stem: Which of the four openings names what is actually in dispute, rather than who happens to be holding the other side of it?

options.text: We agree the scheme is underused, and we disagree about whether that is a design fault or a staffing one
I do not think Ana is right about the scheme, because the numbers she used were the wrong ones
options.misconception: locates the disagreement in a named person rather than in a claim about the scheme

options.text: Ana's presentation was clear and well organised, and I still disagree with its conclusion
options.misconception: praises the speaker in order to avoid saying which claim is actually disputed

options.text: Several people in this room think the scheme is underused, and the rest of us are not convinced
options.misconception: counts positions instead of naming the point on which the members differ

questions.explanation: An opening that names a disagreement lets everyone proceed, because the room can see what is being argued about and therefore who has to answer what. The first option does that, since it fixes the point of agreement and then names the disputed alternative. The second makes the person rather than the claim the object of reply, the third spends a sentence praising the speaker in place of stating the disputed claim, and the fourth reports how many people are on each side, which is a census of the room rather than a description of the disagreement.
questions.hint: Ask which opening tells the room what question the rest of the discussion has to settle.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Counterarguments aimed at a nearby claim
questions.learningObjective: identify a reply that attacks a claim the group did not actually make
questions.stem: A group argues that the seminar should not assign sources longer than ten pages. A member replies: if you object to long texts then you must think students cannot be trusted with anything difficult. What is the specific fault in that reply?

options.text: It has swapped the group's stated limit of ten pages for a general opposition to difficult material, and the passage shows the group never made that claim
It never says what limit should replace ten pages, so the group is left without an alternative to discuss
options.misconception: identifies a real gap in the reply while missing the more basic problem of which claim is being answered

options.text: It puts a question to the group, which turns an objection into something the group has to supply
options.misconception: treats the question form as the fault, when the question is a fair one about the wrong claim

options.text: It accuses the group of thinking students untrustworthy, which the group has never said anything about at all
options.misconception: picks out a single phrase in the reply rather than the substitution the reply actually made

questions.explanation: The group set a boundary at ten pages, and the reply does not attack that boundary, it attacks a view of reading nobody in the group holds, so the group's actual claim survives the exchange untouched while the members argue about a position none of them took. The first option names the substitution. The second and third are real and are worth putting to any reply, since this one does not offer a replacement limit and does phrase the charge as a question, but a perfectly fair question can be asked about the wrong claim, and the fourth isolates a phrase rather than the exchange of one claim for another.
questions.hint: Ask which claim the reply takes itself to be answering, and which claim the group actually made.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Rebuttable and non-rebuttable claims
questions.learningObjective: classify a claim by whether any finding could count against it
questions.stem: Which of the four claims is rebuttable, in the sense that some possible finding would show it to be false?

options.text: Students who see a worked example first make fewer errors on the next problem they attempt
Clearer teaching is better than muddled teaching, other things being equal
options.misconception: states a value comparison, which no finding about the world could show to be false

options.text: Some teaching is better than other teaching, and the seminar ought to aim at the better of them
options.misconception: makes a comparison without naming either the teaching or the outcome being compared

options.text: A good seminar is one in which members are willing to be wrong in front of each other
options.misconception: gives a definition of goodness, which is settled by argument rather than by any finding

questions.explanation: Rebuttability means a specified outcome could have come out the other way, and the first option fixes both the treatment and the outcome, so a student who made more errors afterwards would count against it. The second compares clarity and muddle on the ground of goodness, which is a matter of what the seminar is for rather than of what happened, the third names no outcome at all so nothing could come out otherwise, and the fourth defines a virtue and then recommends pursuing it, which is settled by a group's decision about its own values.
questions.hint: Ask what result would have counted against each claim if it had come out differently.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Tone that closes a discussion
questions.learningObjective: recognise a reply whose form makes further exchange unlikely
questions.stem: A member ends a reply with: at this point I think everyone here can see the only sensible answer. What does that closing move do to the discussion?

options.text: It announces that the matter is settled, so everyone else must now decide whether to press on against a visible verdict
It draws a conclusion, which any speaker is entitled to do once an argument has been made
options.misconception: treats announcing a verdict as a neutral act rather than as a signal to the room

options.text: It uses the word sensible, which is close in meaning to reasonable and so puts no pressure on anyone
options.misconception: reads the phrase as neutral wording and misses what claiming the only answer does to the room

options.text: It appeals to the judgment of the room rather than to evidence, which is the one thing the group lacks here
options.misconception: criticises the appeal to judgment without noticing that the sentence also declares the debate over

questions.explanation: A closing can report where an argument has come to and it can also announce that nothing more will be heard, and the second kind makes the next speaker's job publicly harder than it needs to be, because they must now be the person who reopened a settled matter. The first option describes that effect. The second treats drawing a conclusion as automatically legitimate, the third reads the key word as harmless wording, and the fourth identifies a fair criticism of the appeal to the room's judgment while leaving the announcement itself unexamined.
questions.hint: Ask what the next speaker has to do differently because of the way that reply ended.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Questions used as assertions
questions.learningObjective: recognise a question that carries a conclusion inside its wording
questions.stem: A defender of the new reading list asks the seminar: why keep a compulsory list of eight sources when nobody finishes more than two of them? What kind of question has been asked?

options.text: The wording has already settled that not finishing is the fact and that the list caused it, so the only reply available is a defence of the list's length
The question is genuinely open, since it begins with why and invites any explanation the group can offer
options.misconception: reads the question form as openness and overlooks the conclusion the wording carries

options.text: The question is empirical, since it names a number that a member could go and count if anyone wished to
options.misconception: notices the number and overlooks that the number has been given the job of proof

options.text: The question invites a survey of the members, which would answer it properly within a single afternoon
options.misconception: proposes a method of answering and overlooks what the wording has already assumed

questions.explanation: The question has been built so that a no is nearly impossible, because it presents non-completion as a fact and attaches it to the list, and the only thing left to discuss is why the list is that long. That is a conclusion carried inside a question. The second and third read the surface features, the why-form and the figure of eight, as though they guaranteed openness, when a number quoted by the person asking is being used as proof rather than offered for checking. The fourth proposes how the group might investigate, which is a separate and useful question that this sentence never asks.
questions.hint: Ask which answers to that question would be available to the group.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Disagreements about facts and about values
questions.learningObjective: separate a disagreement about what happened from one about what ought to be valued
questions.stem: One member says the seminar's marking guide is unfair because it rewards long answers. Another replies that the guide is unfair because markers award whatever they happen to feel like awarding. What has happened in this exchange?

options.text: Both members have taken the same charge of unfairness and attached it to a different kind of claim, so the reply does not meet the point made and the group cannot tell who is answering whom
Both members are attacking the marking guide, and the group has no reason to prefer one attack over the other
options.misconception: notices that they share a target and overlooks that the targets are claims of different kinds

options.text: The first member's charge is simply mistaken, since rewarding length is a normal feature of written marking schemes
options.misconception: dismisses one of the two charges instead of noticing that the exchange has missed its own subject

options.text: The second member has conceded the first member's point, since marking down short answers is itself a kind of favouritism
options.misconception: reads a separate criticism as an agreement, and leaves the two claims side by side

questions.explanation: The first charge is about what a good marking scheme ought to reward and the second is about how the markers who use this one actually behaved, and those are different questions that happen to share a word. Because the reply answered a value claim with an observation about conduct, the group has two criticisms of the guide and no exchange, and the second member's factual point has not answered anything the first member said. The second option notes the shared target and misses the shared word, the third dismisses one charge rather than separating the pair, and the fourth invents a concession that was not made.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two charges could both be true and still be about different things.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Interruption that helps and interruption that does not
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an interruption that opens a point from one that closes a thread
questions.stem: A member is halfway through a sentence when another says: hold on, you said earlier that the effect was small, and now you are saying it was large. What makes that interruption productive?

options.text: It takes up something the speaker has already committed to, so the speaker now has to account for the change in their own account
It stops the speaker from finishing, which saves the group from sitting through a long argument to its end
options.misconception: credits the interruption with saving time rather than with exposing something the speaker committed to

options.text: It is phrased as a question, and questions are always more productive than statements in a seminar
options.misconception: treats the question form as the source of the effect instead of the content of the challenge

options.text: It shows the interrupter was paying close attention, which is the first thing a seminar norm requires
options.misconception: credits the interruption with demonstrating attention rather than with doing argumentative work

questions.explanation: An interruption is productive when it puts the speaker's own earlier words in front of them, because the speaker then has to reconcile two positions they have taken, which is work the group cannot do for them. The first option says that. The second treats the interruption as a time-saving device, which is a different and much smaller effect, the third assumes the question form is what does the work when the quoted contradiction is doing it, and the fourth credits the interrupter with showing attention, which is a matter of seminar manners rather than of the argument.
questions.hint: Ask what the speaker now has to do that they would not have had to do otherwise.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Shared premises inside a disagreement
questions.learningObjective: identify a premise both sides already accept while disputing what follows from it
questions.stem: One member says the seminar should not use timed exercises, since they reward speed. Another says the seminar should use them, since without some speed nothing can be covered in the time available. What premise are the two already sharing?

options.text: That what the seminar teaches has to fit the time the seminar has, which is why speed is relevant to both positions
That timed exercises are used in seminars elsewhere, which is why both members know what the form involves
options.misconception: points at shared background knowledge rather than at a premise the conclusion needs

options.text: That the members disagree about timing in particular, which is what makes the exchange look so sharp
options.misconception: reports the visible disagreement as though it were an assumption lying underneath it

options.text: That speed amounts to understanding, which is the belief that makes the question feel urgent to both
options.misconception: names a belief the two members are on opposite sides about rather than one they share

questions.explanation: The two positions are opposites, and the premise that makes them opposites rather than unrelated is the limit on time, since both sides accept that the seminar has a fixed number of hours and both are arguing about what follows from that. The first option states it. The second identifies what the members have in common in the way of background knowledge, which is not doing any work in either argument, the third describes the visible disagreement instead of what lies beneath it, and the fourth names a belief about speed and understanding on which the two members are actually opposed, since one treats speed as the enemy of the thing taught and the other as its instrument.
questions.hint: Ask what both sides must believe for their positions to be opposites rather than merely different.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Quoting the person you disagree with
questions.learningObjective: use an opponent's own words to make them specify what they committed to
questions.stem: A member claims the new marking guide is entirely transparent. A reply says: you said entirely transparent, so you are saying either that the criteria were fixed before marking began or that they were published afterwards. Those are two different claims. What is the reply doing?

options.text: It is using the member's own phrase to draw out the two different claims entirely could stand for, so the member has to say which one was meant
It is citing the guide's own rule about publishing criteria, which shows the member's claim breaks a rule the guide states
options.misconception: describes an appeal to a written rule rather than the request to specify that the reply makes

options.text: It is attacking the word entirely, which is the strongest available objection and the only one the reply needs to make
options.misconception: praises the attack on the adverb and misses the second demand the reply also makes

options.text: It is asking the member to withdraw the claim, which settles the exchange without needing the ambiguity resolved
options.misconception: replaces a request to specify with a demand to withdraw, which is a different move entirely

questions.explanation: The reply takes the member's own sentence and finds that the phrase the member chose covers two different commitments, and then requires the member to say which of them was meant, which is a request the member cannot answer by restating the phrase. The first option names that. The second re-describes the reply as an appeal to a written rule, which is not what the quoted sentence does, the third treats the challenge to the adverb as sufficient and overlooks that the reply also asks for a choice between two claims, and the fourth turns a request to specify into a demand to withdraw, which would let a member escape by saying nothing at all.
questions.hint: Ask what the member has to do next that the member's own wording does not already settle.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A standard of proof changed mid-argument
questions.learningObjective: identify a change in the standard the evidence is being held to
questions.stem: A member argued that the new reporting system has improved student support, citing a satisfaction score that rose from four to five out of five. A colleague said the score rose, but it comes only from students who kept using the service, the students who left never filled anything in, and the system also cut the number of sessions offered per term. The colleague's conclusion is that the system's effect on support is not yet known. What does the colleague change about the first argument?

options.text: The colleague changes what the evidence is being asked to prove, from how high a reported score reached to what such a score can cover once leavers and lost sessions are counted
The colleague adds a second fact about reduced sessions, which strengthens the first member's case rather than limiting it
options.misconception: reads the added fact as support for the original claim rather than as part of a change of standard

options.text: The colleague questions the honesty of the students who did fill in the forms, which is a separate complaint about respondents
options.misconception: turns a problem of coverage into a complaint about the honesty of the people who responded

options.text: The colleague moves the argument to whether the service is good in itself, which is a different dispute from the one being had
options.misconception: shifts the disagreement onto a question the first member never raised and the colleague never asks

questions.explanation: The first member held the score to a standard of level, where a rise from four to five would be sufficient, and the colleague holds the same score to a standard of coverage, where what matters is who was able to answer and what else changed at the same time, and the figures are unchanged between the two. The first option names that shift. The second takes one of the added facts in isolation and reads it as help rather than as part of the wider accounting, the third replaces a coverage problem with dishonesty on the part of respondents, which the colleague never alleges, and the fourth relocates the dispute to a question about the service that nobody in the passage is discussing.
questions.hint: Ask whether the colleague disputes the figures or changes what the figures would have to cover.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Concessions that cost more than they gain
questions.learningObjective: judge whether a concession strengthens a case or removes support from it
questions.stem: A group has argued that its proposal is the only workable one. A member begins the reply: of course, it would be far better to do nothing at all. What has the concession done to the case?

options.text: It granted the proposal's main rival the very merit the case rested on, so the claim of uniqueness has lost what it needed
It showed the group can be fair-minded, which is the quality a seminar most rewards in a speaker
options.misconception: credits the concession with displaying a virtue rather than with changing the argument

options.text: It conceded nothing in substance, since a hypothetical alternative is not a position the group argued against
options.misconception: denies that any concession was made and so leaves the damage to the case unexamined

options.text: It narrowed the argument to what the group can actually show, which is a helpful and proper move here
options.misconception: reads the concession as a useful limiting move rather than as a grant of the rival's merit

questions.explanation: A case for uniqueness needs the alternatives to be worse, so a concession that the alternative is better removes the ground the case was standing on rather than showing the group is fair. The first option says that. The second praises the tone of the reply and leaves the argument untouched, the third insists nothing was conceded, which is exactly the belief that lets a damaging sentence pass, and the fourth reads the sentence as a narrowing, though narrowing would mean conceding that the group cannot show something rather than that its rival is better.
questions.hint: Ask what the case needed to be true about the alternative, and what the concession just said about it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What evidence would have been worth having
questions.learningObjective: identify the finding that would have changed a position the group has now dropped
questions.stem: A group has now dropped its claim that the new marking guide reduces complaints. Which finding would have been worth having before they dropped it?

options.text: Complaint counts from comparable terms that did not use the guide, so the fall could be set beside something to compare it with
More members' opinions about the guide, so the group could see how widely its own claim was shared
options.misconception: supplies more supporters instead of the comparison that a claim about an effect requires

options.text: A description of what the guide asks students to write, so the group could explain the change to them
options.misconception: supplies an explanation aimed at readers rather than any test of whether the claim holds

options.text: A longer history of complaints at the institution, so the group could describe the trend over several years
options.misconception: supplies a longer trend, which still describes complaints rather than testing the guide's effect on them

questions.explanation: The claim was that the guide produced a fall, and a claim about producing a fall needs something to produce the fall against, so the missing finding is a comparison term in which the complaints fell without the guide. The first option names that. The second asks how popular the claim was, which is a matter of agreement rather than of truth, the third explains the change to the people affected, which is worth doing and settles nothing, and the fourth lengthens the description of complaints without ever separating the guide's contribution from anything else in the period.
questions.hint: Ask what the falling numbers would have needed to be falling alongside.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Naming what a reply actually attacks
questions.learningObjective: state a claim and then identify what a given reply is aimed at
questions.stem: A member claims the department should not publish the minutes of its admissions committee. First state the claim, then say what the reply below attacks. The reply: you are assuming that minutes should be secret until somebody shows you a harm. What does that reply attack?

options.text: The assumption that secrecy is the default, which is a premise the claim relies on without ever stating it
The claim itself, by arguing that publication is the better default for a committee of that kind
options.misconception: describes a direct denial of the claim, which the reply in the passage never makes

options.text: The wording of the claim, which is broader than the member meant and could simply be tightened
options.misconception: treats the reply as a complaint about phrasing rather than about a premise underneath it

options.text: The evidence for the claim, which the member has not yet supplied and which the reply declines to ask about
options.misconception: frames the reply as a request for evidence, which is not what the sentence in the passage does

questions.explanation: The reply attacks the default the claim is standing on rather than the claim, since not publishing minutes is treated as the neutral course and the reply wants that neutral course argued for, which is a different and more precise target than the proposal itself. The first option names it. The second turns the reply into a denial the member never made, the third recasts a question about a premise as a matter of phrasing, and the fourth makes it a request for evidence when the sentence asks for an assumption instead, so the group would answer the wrong request if it followed that reading.
questions.hint: Ask what the reply would be satisfied to hear, a withdrawn claim or a defended premise.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Synthesis that changes both positions
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a synthesis that revises both sides from one that averages them
questions.stem: One member wants the seminar to keep written submissions. Another wants every submission discussed aloud. Which outcome is a synthesis rather than a compromise?

options.text: A short written submission sets the agenda and the discussion of it happens aloud, so each side's commitment is kept and both are changed
Written submissions on alternate weeks, so each side gives way once and nobody can say the group refused them
options.misconception: gives each side something it wanted and adds nothing neither side proposed

options.text: Written submissions of half the usual length, which puts the length of submissions midway between the two proposals
options.misconception: adjusts one variable until it sits in the middle, which is arithmetic rather than a new position

options.text: Whichever format the group votes for, since a decision is better than an argument that stays open all term
options.misconception: settles the question by counting rather than by producing a position neither member had held

questions.explanation: A synthesis produces a third position that neither side held and that both can work with, and the first option does that, because putting a short written submission in front of the discussion changes what the first member was asking for and changes what the second was asking for, and each still gets the part they cared about. The second and third divide something up rather than redesign anything, so both members are partly beaten, and the fourth replaces argument with a vote, which produces a decision without producing any new understanding.
questions.hint: Ask whether the outcome could have been proposed by either member before the exchange began.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Duties after being persuaded
questions.learningObjective: state what follows from having accepted another person's reason
questions.stem: A member abandons a position after another member shows her that the group's own figures contradict it. What now follows for her?

options.text: She has to say to the person who changed her mind what did it, since the reason was part of the group's exchange and not a private discovery
Nothing at all, since changing one's mind is a private matter and owes nobody an account of it
options.misconception: treats a change of mind as needing no explanation, which costs the group its ability to check its own reasons

options.text: She should now argue the opposite position, so the group is not left without a view on the question
options.misconception: turns a withdrawn claim into a defended opposite, which is a commitment the member never made

options.text: She should have the figures withdrawn from the seminar's records, so the group is not left working from bad evidence
options.misconception: asks for a change to the archive rather than for an account of her own reasoning

questions.explanation: A reason given in a seminar was offered to the group and not just to her, so the account of being changed belongs in the same exchange, and saying it also lets the group check whether the reason was as good as it seemed. The first option states that. The second is the private view, which loses the group's chance to notice when a good argument is being quietly dropped, the third makes her defend the opposite side, which is not what changing one's mind involves, and the fourth worries about the records rather than about her own position on the question.
questions.hint: Ask where the reason that changed her mind was offered, and to whom it was offered.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Keeping the rejected view in a written synthesis
questions.learningObjective: identify what a synthesis loses when it reports a demand without its reason
questions.stem: A group's written synthesis contains this sentence: the other side wanted longer deadlines, which was unreasonable. What is the specific fault in that sentence?

options.text: It reports the demand and passes judgement on it while leaving out the reason, so a reader cannot tell whether the deadline was refused for good cause or for bad
It dismisses the position with a judgement rather than with an argument, which no synthesis is permitted to contain at all
options.misconception: objects to the presence of a judgement and misses the absence of the reason the judgement rests on

options.text: It paraphrases the other side instead of quoting it, so a reader cannot check the wording that was actually used
options.misconception: objects to the absence of quotation rather than to the absence of the reason behind the demand

options.text: It puts the rejected view second in the sentence, which weights the synthesis in favour of the position that won
options.misconception: objects to the position of the clause, which is a matter of emphasis and not of the reasoning

questions.explanation: A synthesis has to leave a reader able to reconstruct the case that was rejected, and a demand without its reason is the bare minimum, since the reader is left to guess whether the longer deadline was asked for because a member had a care responsibilities nobody had considered or merely to buy more time, and those two demands deserve opposite verdicts. The first option names what is missing. The second objects to the judgement when the real gap is that the judgement has nothing to rest on, the third objects to paraphrasing, which is entirely proper, and the fourth objects to clause order, which is emphasis rather than argument.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader still cannot tell after reading that sentence.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Norms and the mechanisms that enforce them
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a discussion norm from the mechanism that makes it operate
questions.stem: A seminar agrees that no one may use a member's name in order to argue for a position. Which addition turns that agreement into something that actually governs the discussion?

options.text: A stated consequence for a first breach, decided by the group, since a norm with no consequence attached is only an intention
A short written statement of the norm at the head of the reading list, so that everyone can see what was agreed
options.misconception: supplies a record of the norm in place of any consequence for breaking it

options.text: A rule that the chair restates at the start of every session, which keeps the norm in view week after week
options.misconception: adds a reminder rather than a mechanism, since reminding and enforcing come apart here

options.text: A vote at the first meeting, so that the norm carries the authority of a majority decision
options.misconception: confuses agreeing a norm with having any way to act when it is broken

questions.explanation: A norm governs behaviour when the group can do something about behaviour that departs from it, so the missing piece is a consequence the group has agreed to apply, not a statement that the agreement exists. The first option supplies that. The second publishes the rule, which tells members what was agreed and leaves them to work out what happens if they depart from it, the third adds a weekly reminder, which is a way of keeping a norm visible rather than a way of enforcing it, and the fourth settles who agreed, which is a question about authority to decide rather than about what happens next.
questions.hint: Ask what the group would do on the first breach, and whether the group has decided that yet.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Standards of proof across settings
questions.learningObjective: describe how a difference in standard of proof changes what a speaker must show
questions.stem: A court has to satisfy itself that a claim is more likely than not before acting on it, while a seminar asks whether the evidence is good enough to bring into the room. What follows from the difference between those two standards?

options.text: A claim that falls short of a court's standard may still be the right claim to argue in a seminar, because the two settings ask different questions of the same evidence
A claim that falls short of a court's standard is worthless in a seminar, since both settings apply one test
options.misconception: assumes a single standard governs both, which is the very thing the difference denies

options.text: A seminar should apply a stricter test, since an argument that could not survive a court could not survive a room
options.misconception: raises the standard and reverses the direction in which the difference runs

options.text: Neither standard matters, since in the end both are settled by how persuasive the speaker happens to be
options.misconception: makes the question one of speakerly force, which is what a stated standard exists to prevent

questions.explanation: A standard of proof is a rule about what may be done with a claim once the evidence is in, so a court asks whether it is safe to act and a seminar asks whether a claim is worth discussing, and the same evidence can answer yes to the second and no to the first without anyone being wrong. The first option states that. The second treats the two as one test, the third turns the difference around by proposing the stricter standard for the room, and the fourth abandons standards altogether in favour of delivery, which is precisely the outcome a stated standard rules out.
questions.hint: Ask what each setting is going to do with the evidence once it has it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Closings that commit rather than summarise
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a closing that commits to something from one that restates the argument

options.misconception: supplies an assumed attentiveness that the passage nowhere depends on

questions.topic: What makes a next step usable

options.misconception: makes a recap the missing element, which a closing may do but is not required to do

questions.topic: Sequence after abandoning a position
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of retiring a position the group no longer holds
questions.stem: A member has given up a position the group used to hold. Put the steps in the order that lets each one be done properly rather than patched afterwards.

options.text: Say what changed your mind and to whom the account is owed, since the reason was offered to the group
Say what evidence would have been worth having, since that is what tells the group whether the question is settled
State what you hold now, so the group's written positions do not keep an argument nobody makes
Check what else you have written that rested on the position, since a retired argument survives easily in a footnote

questions.explanation: The account comes first, because the reason was offered to the group and the group is entitled to hear that it was good enough to change somebody's mind. Then the missing evidence is named, since that is what tells the room whether the question is now closed or merely better argued. Then the new position is stated, and only then is the group's other writing checked, because a position nobody retires anywhere still does its work quietly in the footnotes of everything else the group has said.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Why a seminar should state its standard of proof
questions.learningObjective: justify fixing a standard of proof before an argument begins
questions.stem: Explain why a seminar should agree a standard of proof before a disagreement starts, rather than arguing about what counts as enough evidence afterwards.

answer.exemplar: A standard of proof is a rule about where a claim's support has to come from, and a seminar that has not agreed one will settle every disagreement by a different route. One member will accept a member's recollection, another will not, a third will not care which and will simply go with the room's mood, and none of them is being unreasonable, because the seminar never told them what the rule was. The cost is not only that the exchange cannot be finished. It is that members cannot tell in advance whether a claim of theirs will be received, so the ones that are harder to support get quietly softened into the ones that are easier, which makes the group less informative over time without anybody deciding to make it so. Agreeing the standard first also makes the disagreement productive when it comes, since both sides know which kind of support is being asked for and a reply can then say that the evidence is the wrong kind, rather than merely that the other side is unconvincing.

questions.explanation: A strong response says that without an agreed rule each member applies a different test and no exchange can be finished, and that the rule also has to exist in advance so that members can tell in advance what will be accepted, which is what stops claims being quietly softened to fit whatever the room will hear.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a member's hard-to-support claim when nobody has said what would count as support.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Why a synthesis must state the view it rejected
questions.learningObjective: justify including the strongest rejected view in a written synthesis
questions.stem: Explain why a written synthesis has to include the strongest version of the view it rejects, rather than summarising the view that won.

answer.exemplar: A synthesis that records only the position it ended up holding is a record of a result, and a result tells a later reader nothing about how hard the alternative was. Someone who reads it and disagrees with the conclusion has no way to discover whether they are disagreeing with a settled question or with a case nobody put properly, and the two situations call for entirely different responses. Stating the rejected view at its strongest is what makes the synthesis checkable, because it gives a reader something they can argue with, and it also constrains the group itself, since a position that has been written out in its best form is one the group will have to answer before it can be filed. The cost is real, since a member whose view is stated at its strongest may be unhappy about it, and the usual way of avoiding that discomfort is to state the view badly. That is precisely the trade the seminar is trying not to make, because a badly stated alternative protects nobody and is the first thing a careful reader notices.

questions.explanation: A strong response says a synthesis that records only the winning view leaves a reader unable to tell whether the question is settled or the case was weak, that stating the rejected view at its strongest is what makes the document checkable, and that the discomfort of seeing your own view stated well is the reason the omission is tempting.
questions.hint: Ask what a later reader can do with a document that reports only the conclusion that was reached.
